newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia disappointed at U.S. trade investigation.
newsitem.headline: Australia disappointed at U.S. trade investigation.

text.p: Australia on Wednesday said it was disappointed at a U.S. decision to investigate its textile clothing, footwear and motor industries under its unfair trade practices law, which can carry punitive action.
"The U.S. action is all the more galling given the range of market access restrictions Australian exporters face into the U.S. market," Trade Minister Tim Fischer said in a statement.

The United States said on Tuesday it would investigate industry schemes in Australia, Argentina, Brazil and Indonesia under its so-called Section 301 trade law that allows retaliation against unfair practices.
In Australia's case, the United States was particularly concerned at the use of export subsidies on leather used in automobile upholstery.

It said Australia, Argentina and Indonesia also would be subject to a U.S. complaint to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) as a result of the industry programmes which it viewed as affecting U.S. carmakers.

Fischer said Australia had approached Washington about the investigations and would defend its position under U.S. domestic law and in the WTO, adding the subsidy schemes were temporary and would be phased out by the year 2000.
"We are very disappointed in this step by the United States and will vigorously defend the (industry) schemes...," he said.
Australia's conservative government, elected in March, has promoted a policy of closer ties with the United States. U.S. President Bill Clinton is due to arrive in Australia in November.
Australia had a substantial trade deficit with the United States and more than A$1.0 billion (US$790 million) of that was the result of U.S. market access restrictions, Fischer said.
Latest figures show Australia had a trade deficit with the United States of A$11.4 billion in 1994/95 ending June 30.
